lesson.title: The Full Picture: Writing Molecular Equations
lesson.summary: Molecular equations show every reactant and product as a complete, neutral compound, giving you the clearest starting point for predicting and balancing chemical reactions.
lesson.body:
When you write a molecular equation, you write every substance in a chemical reaction the way it would appear on a reagent bottle: as a complete, neutral formula, such as NaCl or AgNO3, rather than as separate ions. This is different from how many of these compounds actually behave once they are dissolved in water, where ionic compounds break apart into freely moving cations and anions. A molecular equation is still the right place to start, because it tracks the identity of every substance involved and gives you a formula you can immediately use for stoichiometry: converting between moles, mass, and volume.

Writing a correct molecular equation depends on two skills you have already built. From chemical equations, you bring the rule that atoms are conserved: every element on the left side of the arrow must appear in the same amount on the right side, which you enforce by placing coefficients in front of formulas, never by changing subscripts. From ionic compounds, you bring the rule that formulas must be charge balanced: a compound like calcium chloride is CaCl2, not CaCl, because one Ca2+ ion needs two Cl- ions to cancel its charge, and a compound with a polyatomic ion like sulfate needs parentheses when more than one of that ion is present, as in Al2(SO4)3.

Consider the reaction between solid aluminum and aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Aluminum metal is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from solution, forming copper metal and aluminum sulfate. Writing the correct formulas first, Al, CuSO4, Cu, and Al2(SO4)3, and then balancing atom by atom gives:

2 Al(s) + 3 CuSO4(aq) -> Al2(SO4)3(aq) + 3 Cu(s)

Check it: 2 Al atoms on each side, 3 Cu atoms on each side, and 3 sulfate groups on each side. The state labels, (s) for solid and (aq) for dissolved in water, tell you exactly what you would see in the flask: a piece of gray aluminum metal sitting in a blue copper sulfate solution, slowly being replaced by reddish copper metal as the solution turns colorless.

A balanced molecular equation is also a set of exact mole ratios, and that lets you predict quantities, not just identities. Suppose 5.40 g of aluminum reacts completely with excess copper sulfate solution. How much copper metal forms? First convert mass to moles using aluminum's molar mass: 5.40 g / 26.98 g/mol = 0.2001 mol Al. The balanced equation gives a 2:3 ratio of Al to Cu, so moles of Cu = 0.2001 mol Al x (3 mol Cu / 2 mol Al) = 0.3002 mol Cu. Converting back to mass with copper's molar mass of 63.55 g/mol: 0.3002 mol x 63.55 g/mol = 19.1 g Cu. Every gram of that answer traces back to a correctly written, correctly balanced molecular equation.

This is the habit to build early: write the full, correct formula of every species, balance the equation completely, and only then start doing arithmetic. Every topic ahead, predicting what a reaction will form, identifying an unknown ion in solution, or calculating a concentration from a titration, depends on being able to write this kind of equation quickly and correctly.
